Proposal on opening of Indo-Bangla border 
*61. SHRI R PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government of Bangladesh has sent a proposal to the 
Government to open the Indo-Bangla border for a period of six months on an 
experimental basis; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and argu ments addressed in favour of the 
proposal; and 
(c) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI YASHWANT 
SINHA) (a) No. Sir. 
(b) and (c) Do not arise. 
SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Sir, my question is that, recently, the 
Government of India has given a notification, allowing duty free import of 40 
items, and the Hon. Finance Minister said  that some more items are going to 
be allowed under the Duty Free Arrangement. Sir, it

has been reported in the newspaper—it is The Hindu on May 23, that 
"Bangladesh has proposed that India open its border for six months on an 
"experimental basis" for free access of its products to the latter's markets. 
This proposal is made amid the country's trade deficit to the tune of $1 billion, 
per annum, with India, and limiting Bangladesh exports, to India due to 
imposition of non-tariff and para-tariff barriers." 
Sir, I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether they have made 
any such request. If they have made such a request, what is the response of the 
Government? 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: Sir, As fa r as our trade relations with 
Bangladesh are concerned, we have negotiated with them a Preferential Tariff 
Arrangement under the SAARC process, SAPTA. And bilaterally also, we have 
moved forward with Bangladesh on the Question of Preferential Trade 
Arrangement. It is a fact that Bangladesh , in its trade, has a major imbalance 
because our exports are worth about a billion U.S. dollars; their exports to us are 
about 50-60 million U.S. dollars, and this is a highly surcharged emotional 
issue in Bangladesh. Now, in order to correct this, what we have suggested to 
Bangladesh is that we should have a Free Trade Arrangement as we have had with 
Sri Lanka and that is a Free Trade Arrangement which will take care of this 
problem in a structured, comprehensive and durable basis. I was, Sir, on my 
second visit to Bangladesh in the last twelve months, in Bangladesh on the 14th and 
15th, and I am happy to be reporting to the House, through you, Sir, that the 
Government of Bangladesh has accepted India's suggestion, and they have also 
agreed that the negotiations for the Free Trade Agreement between the two 
countries will begin immediately after the Cancun Ministeria before the middle of 
October. This is the agreement which has been reached. At the same time, when I 
was in Dhaka, the Government of Bangladesh handed over a list of 118 items 
where they suggested to us that we should give them a duty free treatment. We 
have taken note of that suggestion. But I have told the Bangladesh interlocutors 
that it would be better if these things are negotiated with the framework of 
FTA.

SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Sir, in the last few years, in the name of 
regional development cooperation among the SAARC countries, our borders 
are being opened up for free trade. Sir, you would appreciate that India is a 
consumer country. We are the consum ers. Now, from Bangladesh millions

MR. CHAIRMAN: You please come to the question. 
SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: During the recent visit of the hon. Prime 
Minister to China two borders have been opened. We must take some 
precautions; otherwise, we will become a dumping market. What happened 
was that the Gujrat Government had si gned an agreement with Nepal, which

ten years is imported into Nepal every month and it is being dumped into 
India. My question to the hon. External Affairs Minister is: What precautions 
are we taking so that our industry does not suffer? 
Now, Sir, there is a move to open the Myanmar border also. You know 
that through the Myanmar border.. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: There is a question. Let him reply. 
SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA:... a lot of narcotic smuggling is going on. 
In the recent past there was a seizure in Kolkata and a lot of people were

we should be very careful about this. What precautions are you taking. 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: Sir, we are extremely careful and I bring all 
my previous experience here to be able to answer the question that the hon. 
Member has asked. In negotiating free trad e agreements, we take care to have 
a provision about "value added" and this is negotiated as to how much value 
should be added, whether it should be 50 per cent or whether it should be 60 
per cent or whether it should be 80 per cent, and the "value added" takes care of 
the problem that if that country with which we have an agreement is importing 
something and we export it wit hout adequate value added, then, that will not 
qualify for duty free treatment. This is one point, Sir. The other is, you look at 
our tariffs. Our tariffs are also coming down. In case the tariff regime itself is 
harmonised to an extent, that takes care of cheaper import of raw materials 
and even finished goods. At the same time, I must also say that what we are 
trying to create in South Asia is a win-win situation for all the countries in 
this region. India, as the largest country, must play its role very responsibly, 
as a promoter of this concept of cooperation between the SAARC countries in 
the region. This is the broader vision that we have and this must always be kept 
in mind. So far as the question on vanaspati and other things is concerned, we 
have even been permitted by the WTO the concept of tariff quota where we 
say only so much can be imported duty free and the rest will have to pay duty. 
There are various protections in the trade regime which take care of the 
problems that the hon. Member has raised.

SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY: I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister whether the trade agreement that we are working out with 
Bangladesh is contingent on reciprocal undertaking by bangladesh to allow 
free transit of Indian goods through Bangladesh to the North East. 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: It is not contingent on transit and 
transhipment. But this is an issue that we have raised with Bangladesh right 
from the beginning. There are agreem ents between India and Bangladesh 
entered into in 1972, reiterated in 1973, reiterated in 1980, reiterated in 1997 
and 1999 where they have agreed to give us transit and transhipment rights. 
But the transit and transhipment right, as the hon. House might be aware, is 
mainly through the inland water route. So  far as railway and road transits are 
concerned, Bangladesh's point has been that it is not fit enough or strong 
enough or adequate enough to be able to take the load of the transit of goods 
which will move from one part of India to another. This is something that we 
are continually discussing with them. The reply to the question is the two are 
not contingent on each other.

Statement 
Prime Minister participated in the G-8 Enlarged Dialogue in Evian on 1st 
June 2003 at the invitation of Presiden t Chirac. There wa s a free and frank 
exchange of views on development assistance to developing countries, transfer 
of technologies, environment related issues and trade barriers that affect 
developing countries. The Enlarged Dialogue was the first of its kind and was 
not intended to produce a formal Summit document. Its intention was to 
articulate concerns of developing countries and exchange views with developed 
countries on the above issues. 
PM expressed disappointment at the lack of progress so far on the 
Millennium Development Round since the Doha meeting. PM underlined the 
need to eliminate tariff and non-tariff barriers, especially phasing out all trade 
distorting agricultural subsidies, removal of restrictions on the free movement 
of natural persons for providing serv ices and broader access of developing 
countries to pharmaceuticals. 
The issues raised by PM were also re flected in the statements of some of 
the other developing country participants in the Enlarged Dialogue. While 
there was no formal comment by the G8 on the issues

High technology cooperation with U.S. 
*67. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Prime Minister during his visit to New York 
in last September referred to the scope in high technology co-operation; and 
(b) if so, the details if fields where such co-operation has started? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) and (d) During their meeting in 
New York on 12 September 2002, Prime Minister and U.S. President George 
W. Bush agreed to explore possibilities of expanding cooperation in space, 
diverse forms of energy, high-technology commerce and science. 
India and the United States have initiated five safety related projects for 
safeguarded nuclear facilities. Exchange of visits by U.S. and Indian nuclear 
regulatory officials has also commenced . In the area of space, the two sides 
have renewed the Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation in earth 
and atmospheric sciences. The United States has offered to resume co-
operation in space, appli cations for sustainable development, whether 
research missions, tele-medicine, tele-education and disaster management. 
Joint workshops on civilian space application and research have also started. 
The two sides have established a bilateral High Technology Cooperation 
Group, which held its first meeting in Washington D.C. on 1 -2 July 2003. 
This is the first such group that the United States has set up with any country. 
The Group discussed regulatory and promotional issues related to enhancing 
trade in 'dual use' goods and technologies, as well as facilitating cooperation 
in areas such as information technolo gy, life sciences, nano-technology and 
defence technology. 
The two sides are also pursuing co llaborative science and technology 
projects in the areas of health and communicable diseases, environment and 
climate change, and renewable and clean energy. Under the aegis of the 1998 
agreement between Department of Science and Technology and the U.S. 
National Science Foundation, there are currently about 65   scientific 
research projects supported by various labs,

institutions and universities in India and U.S.A. The India-U.S. Science and 
Technology Forum was established in 2000 to catalyse India-U.S. scientific 
collaboration.

524. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to 
state": 
(a) whether the Second Labour Commission's recommendations to 
"rationalise" labour laws for liberalisation are being processed and any time-
frame has been evolved to conclude this exercise;

Conference and several seminars held during the last year, have been 
consolidated; and

Commission's recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) The Second National Commission on Labour 
(NCL) in its report submitted to the Government on 29.06.2003 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2003] 
had made wide-ranging recommendati ons on various facets of labour viz. 
review of laws, social security, women & child labour, skill development, wages, 
labour administration, unorganised sector, etc. The recommendations have 
been receiving utmost attention of the Government. The Ministry has already 
held detailed consultations and interactions with the workers representatives, 
employers organisations, experts & professionals etc. The Report of the 
Commission was discussed at the 38th Session of Indian Labour Conference 
held on 28-29 September, 2002, a National Seminar on Unorganised Sector 
Workers on 7-8 November 2002 and a Tripartite Committee Meeting held on 
18-19 February 2003. Such initiatives are necessary to evolve cosensus for

employment generation, bringing attitudinal change with emphasis on 
participative management and consolidation of social security legislation and 
establishment of social security sytstem.

532. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Second Labour Commission's recommendations to 
rationalise labour laws for liberalisation has not made any progress for 
the last one year;

Industrial Disputes Act, 1947  is being contemplated in the light of NCL's

SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL: Madam, I have great pleasure in 
introducing this Motion. The purpose of introducing this Motion is to review 
ten years of implementation of the Part IX and IX-A of the Constitution 
dealing with Panchayats and Municipalities as institutions of self-
government. The Constitution (73 rd Amendment) Act, 1992 dealing with 
Panchayats, which came into force with effect from 24 th April, 1993 is a 
landmark in the history of Panchayats.   With this amendment a three-tier 
structure of governance 
203 

 
RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2003] 
was introduced in the rural areas of our federal polity. Elections were made 
compulsory every five years to the th ree tiers. Reservations were introduced 
for SCs/STs and Women and a separate domain of 29 subjects was listed out 
for the Panchayats to function. 
Today, ten years after the passing of the 73rd Amendment Act, after a 
lot of efforts, we have been able to achieve regular conduct of elections, give 
effect to reservation of seats for Sc heduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and 
Women, appoint State Finance Commissions and State Election 
Commissions. Panchayat elections have been heid in all the States, except 
Jharkhand and the Union Territory of Pondicherry. We have around 2.50 lakh 
Panchayats of which about 2.25 lakh are Gram Panchayats. Approximately 30 
lakh persons have been elected to these Panchayats of whom more than 10 
lakh are women giving us the largest representative base anywhere in the 
world. While appreciating the efforts so far made by our State Governments in 
enacting the required legislations in their respective States to implement the 
provisions of the 73rd Amendment Act, 1993, I have to stress that still a lot of 
ground has to be covered to strengthen Panchayati Raj Institutions. Much 
remains to be done in the field of devolution of financial and administrative 
powers to Panchayats. While some States have devolved powers on 
Panchayats, many others are yet to make a beginning. States which devolved 
powers vary in the extent and type of devolution. While some States have 
devolved more powers upon District and Intermediate Panchayats, some 
others have devolved powers only on the Gram Panchayats and Intermediate 
Panchayats, ignoring the District Panchayats. Most States, after devolving 
several responsibilities on the PRIs, have not transferred the requisite staff and 
funds in respect of the subjects transf erred to Panchayats, which are essential 
to carrying out the responsibilities entrusted on them. Besides, Panchayats 
must be given commensurate powers to levy and collect their own taxes, and 
generate their own resources. Only wh en resources are made available and 
administrative powers given to Panchayats, would they be able to take care of 
local level needs and function as institutions of self government. 
States are also found to be wanting in constituting District Planning 
Committees, holding regular Gram Sabha meetings and building in 
accountability of Panchayats. There is also a need for revamping and aligning 
the election machinery, the audit mach inery and the Finance Commissions in 
the States to bring them in line with their counterpart institutions at the 
Centre. 
204 

(24 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
To enable the institution of Panchayats to function in an effective 
manner, the Gram Sabhas have to be vested with responsibilities such as 
supervision and monitoring the functioning of the Gram Panchayats, approval 
of plans and selection of beneficiaries and projects, mobilization of 
contribution in cash or kind such as voluntary labour for community welfare 
projects and promotion of unity and harmony among all sections of society. 
Gram Sabhas have yet to be empowered in an effective manner in most 
States.

The provisions of Panchayats (Extension to the Schedule V Areas) Act, 1996 
extends the provisions of the 73 rd Amendment Act to Schedule V Areas to 
give the benefit of local self-government to predominantly tribal areas. The 
PESA Act provides, that every legislation on the Panchayats in Schedule V 
Areas should be in conformity with the customary laws, social and religious 
practices and traditional management of community resources. It provides for 
100 per cent reservation for Scheduled Tribes for the seat of Chairpersons at 
all levels of the Panchayats and proportionate but not less than 50 per cent of 
the total number of seats of Members to be reserved for Scheduled Tribes in 
all tiers of Panchayats. The Act vests wide ranging powers in the Gram 
Sabhas in Scheduled Areas such as mandatory consultations with Gram 
Sabha prior to land acquisition, entrustment of planning and management of 
water bodies to Gram Sabha, mandatory requirement of Gram Sabha 
recommendations for grant of prospec ting licence or mining lease or for 
exploration of minor minerals. The Act also vests in the Gram Sabha the 
power to enforce prohibition to restrict the sale and consumption of 
intoxicants. It vests in the Gram Sabha the ownership of minor forest 
produce, powers to manage village markets; to exercise control over money-
lending to the Scheduled Tribes; and control local plans and resources 
including tribal sub plans. The PESA Act extends to Tribal Areas of nine 
States, namely. Andhra Pradesh, Chha ttisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh,

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE : Thank you, Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, for permitting me to make some observations on the motion 
moved by the hon. Minister. A period of ten years, after the passage of the 
Seventy-third and Seventy-fourth Amendments to the Constitution, is, no 
doubt, a milestone in the process of consolidating the democratic structure of 
this country. Naturally, on this occasion our mind goes to that young man, 
who not only dreamt of the 21 st century but also visua lised that, to play an 
effective role in the 21 s1 century, there was a need to re-organise institutional 
structures and, primarily, to strengthen our basic democratic structure. Surely, 
I do feel that this House would be failing in its duty, if we do not gratefully 
remember the contributions made by late Rajiv Gandhi in strengthening the 
democratic structure of this country. After the Constitution was adopted in the 
early '50s, exactly speaking, on 26 th January, 1950--the work of drafting the 
Constitution was completed in November, 1949-there has been a sea-change. 
The type of democratic structure, whic h was contemplated at that point of 
time, was to have one Central Government and several Provincial" 
Governments. Of course, in the early years of our Reoublic we had different 
categories of States, ranging from Part-A  State to Part-D State. Nonetheless, 
the basic concept of our federation was that the Federal Government and the 
constituent units would enjoy power from the Constitution itself to play their 
role in the service of the nation. Toda y, when we are celebrating the tenth 
y6ar of Seventy-third and Seventy-f ourth Amendments to the Constitution, 
our population has increased by three times.    There are tremendous 
technological changes.

approving layouts, taking up work up to Rs. 1 lakh from the General Fund 
and can engage private engineers for speedy execution of work, etc. 
Intermediate Panchayat is vested with power of maintenance of roads, 
dispensaries, elementary schools and execution of development programmes. 
District Panchayat is empowered with planning, coordination and advisory 
functions, identification of works und er the Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar 
Yojana. The State Finance Commission grants and the SGRY funds are 
provided to the District Panchayats for community level projects. 
Sir, the Government of Tamil Nadu, under the leadership of Dr. 
Puratchithalaivi is implementing the various provisions of the 73 rd 
Amendment and the 74 th Amendment in true letter and spirit which have 
borne fruit and improved the conditions of the people of Tamil Nadu 
significantly and emerged as a model institution of self-government. Thank 
you, Sir. 
SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU (Pondicherry): Thank you, Sir, 
for having given me this opportunity to speak on this Motion. I welcome the 
Motion. The 73 rd Amendment in the Constitution generated enthusiasm 
among the people. They thought that th ere will be a larger  participation of 
rural people, there will be democracy at  the grassroot level and there will be 
decentralisation of power throughout  India and the people would rule 
themselves. This was the slogan which was envisaged after the 73 rd 
Amendment. Even though the amendment has been made, the reality is that 
the Panchayats are toothless. 
Sir, I would like to read from a recent survey of Panchayats working 
in 19 States, conducted by the National Institute of Rural Development. It 
states as under: 
1) Absence of a national consensus across party lines on what 
should be the status of the PRIs. There has been no political 
initiative to empower the Gram Sabha (village council 
consisting of all voters) and to get the PRIs back on track 
for speedy rural development. 
2) High-level political authorities are unwilling to give up 
control over finance and development schemes.

3) The stronghold of the bureaucracy over PRIs continues. 
4) Functional and financial autonomy has not been granted to 
the PRIs. 
5) PRIs are perceived as lower-level agencies of the 
government, diluting their conceived status as units of self-
government. 
6) There is a tendency to execute only schemes sponsored by 
the State or Union Government. Hardly any programmes 
are carried out from PRIs own resources. 
7) Most States have failed to give the Gram Sabha a mandate 
by clearly defining its functions and authority. This renders 
the Gram Sabha ineffective. 
8) There has been no transfer of general or technical staff by 
the State Governments to the PRIs. 
So, Sir, these are the eight defects which have been pointed out, and 
it is said that the Panchayats are toothless. Taking these facts into 
consideration. I believe the Government of India would like to make an 
amendment to the Constitution for strengthening the Panchayat system, as it 
is. 
Sir, I would further like to say that several district planning 
commissions have to be constituted as per the provisions of article 243(d) of 
the Constitution. It has already been said by Mr. Reddy that the DPCs are 
entrusted with the job of preparing composite plan, but it has to be headed by 
the elected bodies. What has happened is this. In certain States, Ministers 
have been appointed; in certain St ates, bureaucrats alone have been 
appointed; in certain States committees have not even been constituted. So, 
this is the tendency which is prevailing. 
Another thing I would like to say is, even when the Gram Panchayat 
is already constituted, the State Governments are interfering with their affairs 
by appointing parallel committees. The parallel committees are like water-
sharing committees, vigilance committees, village prohibition committees 
and village education committees. Thes e committees are, more or less, 
functioning as parallel Village Panchayat Committees, causing a lot of 
hindrance. The Prime Minister has also cautioned certain States saying 
253 

RAJYA SABHA      [24 July, 2003] 
not to constitute parallel committees which cause hindrance to the working of 
Panchayats. 
I have another worry and I would like to submit that before the 
august House. The Government of India has the Ministry of Rural 
Development. This Ministry is pumping crores of rupees to the Village 
Panchayats. This too is, more or less, working parallel to the Panchayats. The 
Ministry of Rural Development is pumping money like anything into the 
villages and this Ministry is functioning, more or less, parallel to the Village 
Panchayats. Instead of doing that, you assign all the functions to the Village 
Panchayats; let them do it as they want. Above all, the Rural Development 
Ministry has constituted District Vigilance and Monitoring Committees 
appointing Members of Parliament as the Chairmen of those committees. My 
worry is, on the one hand, we say not to constitute any committees that 
interfere with the working of Village Panchayats. On the other hand, we 
constitute committees like this and this, more or less, interferes with the 
working of the Village Panchayats. I request the hon. Minister to consider this 
aspect. You must ask the State Governme nts also not to encroach upon the 
working of Village Panchayats. I also request the Central Government not to 
interfere with the working of the Village Panchayats. 
I have another submission. In certain States, we are not able to 
conduct elections that are reserved for Scheduled Castes. What is the reason? 
In Tamil Nadu and several other places, elections are not conducted in places 
reserved for SCs because the SC peopl e are landless poor agriculturists, 
depending upon the caste Hindus. They also fear economic boycott. They fear 
that the economic boycott may be enforced against the dalit people, and that is 
why they are afraid of contesting electio ns. Moreover, they are landless, poor 
agricultural people and they don't want to have any quarrel with the rich 
agriculturists. On those grounds, they  are not able to contest elections. I 
request the Government to provide adequate security for those who want to 
contest elections. There should be a strong action against those who prevent 
dalits from contesting elections. Even after they get elected, they have been 
prevented from continuing in office, they resigned and went away. The civil 
society also should come forward to help those people. 
I would like also to say that we are making several amendments. 
Evert the Supreme Court has recently delivered a judgment in regard to 
254 

[24 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Members of Parliament and Legislativ e Assemblies, laying down what are 
the things the applicants should d eclare, at the time of filing their 
nominations. They have to declare their assets, their convictions and 
educational qualification. This also should be stipulated for those who want 
to contest Panchayat elections. It shou ld be incorporated in respect of 
Panchayat elections also. A person who wants to contest elections should 
declare all these facts before becoming a member of any body. I request the 
Minister to kindly take this into consideration. 
There is another thing to be considered. If a ruling party is in power 
in a particular State, and if the Opposition's party has won the election for 
Mayor's post, or, Chairman of any Village Panchayat or municipality, we are 
having a lot of difficulties. They are not getting financial assistance. Everyday, 
they are being humiliated. Everyday, they are being charged, and they are 
facing problems in the day-to-day functioning. A sort of pandemonium has 
been created. It should not be allowed to continue as it is now. In order to 
avoid this anomaly, there should be some law. If the elected bodies are 
headed by opposition parties, they also should be allowed to function without 
fear, and all kinds of facilities should be provided to them by the ruling party. 
If an agitation goes on in a State, now the Central Government says, "No, it is 
the State Government's job, we can't interfere." The same thing should be 
applied for the Panchayats also by the State Governments, even if they are 
ruled by opposition parties. The State Government should say, "We are not 
going to interfere with it, since it is a subject of the concerned municipalities 
and corporations." 
With these words, I support the motion. Thank you.

SHRI R.S. GAVAI (Maharashtra): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, at the 
outset, I welcome the Motion moved by the hon. Minister, Mr. Patil, to 
consider the progress of the Panchayats and Municipalities as institutions of 
self-government during the last ten years. 
It does mean also that, while discussing about the progress of the Panchayat 
Raj, an inherently impression is that he is inviting some suggestions from us 
for the better implementation of the Act. Sir, coming to the Constitution 
(Seventy-third) Amendment Act, 1992, I would say that I will cover only four 
aspects. As an example, I deal with the progress of it and thereafter give some 
suggestions. The first aspect is Gram Sabha. The second aspect is District 
Planning and Development Committee. The third aspect is Extension to the 
Scheduled Area. The fourth and the last aspect is the subject given in the 
Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution. Sir, what is the purpose of the 
Constitution (Seventy-third) Amendment Act? It gives a constitutional status 
to Gram Sabha. Gram Sabha means a bo dy consisting of persons, registered 
in the electoral rolls, relating to a village comprised within the area of 
panchayat at the village level, Gram  Sabha may exercise such power and 
perform such functions at the village level as the Legislature of a State may, 
by law, provide. That is how villager, above the age of eighteen years, has an 
inherent right to determine his own destiny. Gram Sabha is the forum where 
the marginalized poor can influence th e decisions affecting their life. I do 
refer, of course, to the very purpose given in the Constitution, I would give 
the gist.    The role of the

Panchayat Raj institution at the village level. The role of the local people in

Gram Panchayat has a Gram Sabha in Ma harashtra; whether all the citizens,

this is being spoiled because of faulty implementation. Sir, it is my habit that 
whenever I go to a public function, I go to the Gram Panchayat or to the 
Sarpanch concerned and ask them to show me the register which has to be 
maintained by them to record the number of people, living below poverty line.

to find out who is at the helm of affairs, not to allow the people of villages to

'below poverty line' is the basis for the prospective progress of the people,

criterion for these schemes? The criteri on is that the individual beneficiary

for the last ten years in our country. A constitutional protection has been 
given to it, so that throughout the country it could be implemented in a 
uniform way so as to have the decentralis ation of power in this country. I feel 
the real intention or the real spirit of this Panchayati Raj and Nagar Palika 
Institutions in Part IX and Part-IX-A of the Constitution is very specific in 
this matter. But let us analyse the experience which we have gained during the 
last ten years. According to my pe rsonal experience -- I was a Gram 
Panchayat member, subsequently I was elected to the Zila Panchayat and 
District Council, which was just now referred to by the hon. Member, Shri 
V.V. Raghavan -- wherever there is a Government which is having the 
political will of having decentralisation of  power, there it is implemented in a 
proper way. That is the real thing which has happened. In those States where 
the Government or State authorities were not interested in devolution of 
powers or not interested in parting w ith the powers which were entrusted to 
them, nothing has been done so far. This is what we have been experiencing 
for the last ten years. I can cite so many examples, but due to paucity of time I 
am not going into all those things. Sir, the reason is that almost in all the 
provisions in Part IX and Part-IX-A of the Constitution or in the 73 rd and 74th 
Amendments, so many discretionary powers are being vested with the State 
Legislatures to enact laws. That loophol e is being made use of by the State 
Governments in order to cr eate hurdles in the decentr alisation of power. That 
is why the Panchayati Raj Institutions are not being empowered with 
functions, functionaries and funds, as was rightly mentioned by Pranabda. 
That is what has happened in this country. For example, article 243 (g) is the 
cardinal provision in the 73 rd Constitution Amendment, i.e., the State may 
enact a law as far as the powers to be or the subjects to be transferred to the 
Panchayati Raj Institutions are concerned.  There are 29 subjects. But that is 
subject to the discretion and whims and fancies of the State 
287 

RAJYA SABHA       [24 July, 2003] 
Legislature as the Government thinks it fit. That means when discretion is 
absolute upon the State Government where they are interested in devolution of 
power, they can transfer it. Going through the chart which is annexed with the 
background paper, it is very clear that  even now so many States are having 
powers with them. It is just like that they are still holding those powers. So, 
my humble suggestion to the hon. Minister through you, Sir, is that these

particular State is not functioning properly. Therefore, the Government should 
intervene. This is a three-tier administration. The Panchayati Raj 
adminsitration or Nagar Palika administration is the grassroot of Indian 
democracy. Strengthening the Panchayati Raj institution means, we are 
strengthening rural India. Strengthening the rural India means, we are

Indian democracy. Suppose, any State or any authority is not willing to oblige

remedy. If we have some remedy, then, it should be a mandatory provision.

Regarding the review of this, I do appreciate that the Scheduled 
Castes and the Scheduled Tribes and the women have got the benefits. There 
are periodical elections, transfer or devolution of powers and the District 
Planning Committees. How the District Planning Committee is misused,

the charge of the Chairm an of the District Planning Committee. Is this 
decentralisation? Is this decentralisati on or centralisation? That is why I am 
suggesting that all these provisions have to

Sir, I would like to cite another defect in the 73 rd and the 73 th
